papers.title: Holocene ecosystem succession and fire regime evolution at Tannersville Bog, northeastern United States
papers.abstract: Abstract. Northern peatlands are among the largest long-term terrestrial carbon reservoirs on Earth, with carbon accumulation jointly regulated by climate, hydrological conditions, and vegetation composition. Future climate warming is expected to accelerate the transition from lakes to peatlands while increasing the likelihood of peatland fires, which can rapidly release carbon accumulated for millennia. However, our understanding of how fire and peatland ecosystem development co-evolve over millennial timescales remains poorly understood. Tannersville Bog (TANB), a temperate boreal peatland in northeastern Pennsylvania, provides an ideal natural laboratory for investigating how northern peatlands are shaped and affected by fire, post-glacial ecosystem succession, and climate. Here, we integrate pyrogenic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (pyroPAHs), n-alkane biomarkers, and sediment composition analyses to reconstruct the Holocene fire and environmental changes of TANB. The combined proxy records identify four major stages of ecosystem succession, from a shallow lake to a rich fen, a fen–bog transitional system, and ultimately a Sphagnum-dominated bog. Correspondingly, multivariate classification of PAH assemblages identifies four distinct fire regimes, which we link to vegetation and peatland-development proxies through ordination analyses. These fire regimes evolved alongside ecosystem succession, reflecting shifts in fuel composition, combustion processes, and fire-source characteristics. The lake-to-peatland transition also reveals that changing depositional and preservation conditions influenced PAH distributions without obscuring major fire-regime transitions. Our results demonstrate that long-term fire-regime evolution was jointly controlled by changes in vegetation composition, peatland hydrology, and basin development, highlighting strong mutual feedback between ecosystem succession and fire over millennial timescales.

papers.title: Region-specific time lags in the response of black carbon to ENSO from 46 years of MERRA-2 reanalysis
papers.abstract: Abstract. The relationship between El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and global black carbon (BC) loading is not described by a single timescale. Using 46 years (1980 to 2025) of MERRA-2 reanalysis, we regress BC column mass anomalies against the Oceanic Niño Index at lags of 0 to 12 months at every grid point, accounting for autocorrelation and applying false discovery rate (FDR) correction. BC responds to ENSO on region-specific lags: near zero over the Maritime Continent, about five months over Central America, and seven to eight months over the Amazon. These lags are reproduced in 1980 to 2009 and 2010 to 2025, periods driven by different biomass burning emission inventories, so the timing is not an artifact of the inventory or of the 1997 to 1998 El Niño, and it is consistent with the pan-tropical cascade of fire anomalies documented in satellite fire records. No relationship is detectable over the continental United States, central Africa, or Siberia in either period; over the continental United States, the largest full-record median correlation (0.03) is about one fifth of the smallest detectable correlation, partly because weak correlations of opposite sign in the two periods cancel. The fraction of grid points passing FDR correction changes abruptly between adjacent lags while correlation strength varies smoothly, so response timing is better read from correlation magnitude than from significance counts. Anticipating ENSO-driven aerosol loading therefore requires resolving when the relationship emerges in each region, not only whether it exists.

papers.title: Water management in flood-prone areas using nature-based solutions: an AI-assisted systematic review and thematic analysis
papers.abstract: Nature-based solutions (NbS) are increasingly used to reduce flood risk and improve water management in flood-prone areas. However, research remains fragmented across disciplines, regions, and scales, making it difficult to identify research trends, knowledge gaps, and priorities. This study presents an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted systematic review of peer-reviewed articles published between 2016 and 2025, retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, a large language model (LLM) was used to screen titles and abstracts, followed by full-text review by the research team. A structured dataset was developed through LLM-assisted data extraction and human validation. Semantic clustering and LLM-assisted synthesis were then used to identify research themes and summarize implementation conditions, benefits, limitations, and research needs. A total of 185 studies were included, which were predominantly published between 2021 and 2025. Nine research themes emerged, with urban green infrastructure for runoff mitigation, spatial planning and decision support, and catchment and hydraulic modeling accounting for 47.6% of the studies. Research was concentrated in the United Kingdom, China, and the United States, with limited representation from Africa and Latin America. The evidence relied mainly on scenario modeling and short monitoring periods, while social equity, public acceptance, and maintenance outcomes were rarely assessed using standardized metrics. While literature reviews have been previously done on the topic of NbS for flood-prone water management, to our knowledge, this is the first review of NbS for flood-prone water management to combine LLM-assisted screening, data extraction, and synthesis with semantic clustering and human validation. The study provides a thematic evidence map, examines temporal and geographic research trends, and presents a reproducible workflow to support future environmental evidence synthesis.

papers.title: Regional moisture conditions and mid- to late-Holocene wildfire variability along the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau
papers.abstract: Wildfire is a major disturbance in terrestrial ecosystems. Previous studies have shown that since the Last Glacial Maximum, wildfire activity across the East Asian and Indian summer monsoon regions has been closely associated with precipitation variability on suborbital to millennial timescales. However, continuous records of long-term wildfire dynamics and their relationships with regional moisture variability remain scarce in the alpine regions along the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau. In this study, a composite fire activity index (FAI) was constructed by integrating the fluxes of levoglucosan (Lev), mannosan (Man), and galactosan (Gan) measured in a sediment core from Wodi Co, northwestern Yunnan, China. The molecular wildfire record was evaluated together with paleolimnological proxies (Ca/Si, Fe/Mn, Zr/Rb, total organic carbon (TOC) and >64 μm grain-size fraction), TraCE21k-simulated moisture-related climate variables, and records of large-scale atmospheric circulation to reconstruct regional wildfire variability over the past approximately 4.5 kyr. The results indicate that wildfire activity was particularly intense between ∼2.9 and 2.0 kyr BP. During this interval, enhanced lake-water concentration, more oxic sedimentary conditions, and reduced precipitation collectively point to regional drought, while sedimentary organic-carbon accumulation remained relatively low. These findings suggest that wildfire activity was primarily associated with the regional moisture variability in the alpine area of northwestern Yunnan, consistent with paleofire records from southern and southwestern China. From a large-scale circulation perspective, variability in the Indian summer monsoon and ENSO may have jointly influenced the climatic background of wildfire season moisture conditions. Since 2 kyr BP, wildfire activity has generally remained low, broadly consistent with the widespread monsoon reorganization and the shift towards wetter conditions recorded across the Asian monsoon domain. This study provides new sedimentary evidence for understanding long-term linkages between wildfire activity and regional moisture conditions along the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau.

papers.title: How do weather, topography and fuel condition drive the extreme behavior of a Mediterranean megafire? A case study of the 2025 Jarilla wildfire (western Spain)
papers.abstract: The 2025 wildfire season was the most destructive on record in the European Union, with more than 1 million hectares burned, and the Iberian Peninsula was the hardest-hit region, accounting for 43% of that area. The Jarilla wildfire (Cáceres, Spain; 17,317 ha, august 2025) exemplifies how meteorology, topography, and fuel condition jointly controlled the behavior of these Iberian megafires. Our aim was to analyze the role of these three factors in the fire’s behavior and to evaluate their interpretation against the post-fire severity footprint, within a reproducible workflow relying entirely on open-access data. We combined ERA5 hourly reanalysis, the fire weather index (FWI), Sentinel-2 spectral indices (NDVI, NDII, dNBR), VIIRS active-fire detections, and the 5 m PNOA digital elevation model. During the active phase (august 12–17), the atmosphere was extremely desiccating—vapor pressure deficit peaking at 5.9 kPa, minimum relative humidity near 15%, and FWI in the “extreme” class—acting on a dense but already water-stressed fuel cover (mean NDVI 0.53, mean NDII 0.05). The wind regime was bimodal: a frequent but weak nocturnal north-easterly flow and a diurnal south–south-westerly (SSW) flow that drove the observed SW–NE progression. Fire spread corridors—steep, wind-aligned, fuel-laden terrain delineated with the SSW driving wind—covered 13.7% of the burned area and showed higher mean severity (dNBR 665) than their surroundings (525); however, 84% of the high-severity area lay outside them. These results indicate that, in such “hot-drought” megafires, severity is driven primarily by extreme atmospheric drying acting on continuous, dry fuel, whereas topography and wind spatially organize its peaks rather than determining them. Beyond reconstructing a single event, the study provides a transferable, open-data framework for diagnosing megafire drivers and suggests that fuel- and weather-based prevention, more than topographic targeting, is key to mitigating Mediterranean megafires.

papers.title: Fire Regime in Wasur National Park, Indonesia: Climatic Influences and Indigenous Burning Practices
papers.abstract: This study examines the fire regime and its driving factors in Wasur National Park, Indonesia. This study employs a MODIS hotspot time-series analysis to examine the relationship between hotspot detections and climatic variables, supported by in-depth interviews with key informants from Kanume, an indigenous people living in Wasur NP. The findings reveal that the monsoonal climate, with its distinct dry and wet seasons, is strongly associated with annual variations in hotspot detection. From 2000 to 2023, hotspot detections were concentrated in the dry season, beginning in May-July, peaking in September-October, and declining in November-December when the wet season began. Pearson correlation analysis indicated that rainfall, number of rainy days, wind speed, and relative humidity are all associated with hotspot detections, whereas temperature shows a negligible relationship. El Niño and La Niña anomalies are linked to interannual variations in hotspot detections. Beyond climatic factors, Indigenous fire-use practices tied to local livelihoods provide a plausible anthropogenic pathway for burning. Based on Kanume's seasonal calendar, traditional burning commonly occurs during Tebrasaro and Sep-Sep; however, changes in burning practices and environmental conditions may increase the likelihood of less controlled fires. Beyond proximate climatic and human fire -use practices, fire activity patterns in Wasur NP reflect broader socio-ecological processes shaped by political-economic transformations and governance systems. These findings highlight the importance of fire governance approaches that recognize Indigenous fire governance systems and strengthen collaboration between state and customary institutions.

papers.title: Extreme temperatures and the epithelial barrier theory
papers.abstract: Extreme temperatures are now recognized as significant global health threats, driving morbidity and mortality across diverse diseases by compromising epithelial barrier integrity and causing periepithelial inflammation. The epithelial barrier theory posits that environmentally induced barrier dysfunction, driven by modern industrial and urban exposures, leads to compromised surfaces of the exposed tissues accompanied by epithelial activation and barrier dysfunction, microbial dysbiosis, loss of commensal bacteria, opportunistic pathogen colonization, bacterial translocation, inflammation and immune dysregulation. While toxic chemical exposures have been the primary focus of barrier research, temperature extremes-now intensified by anthropogenic warming, altered weather patterns and regional climatic variability-may similarly disrupt epithelial structure and function. Heat and cold can alter tight-junction regulation, induce mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, apoptosis and modify cytokine and chemokine profiles, thereby weakening barrier defenses and enhancing susceptibility to pollutants, allergens and pathogens. These effects may be amplified by co-exposures such as humidity fluctuations, UV radiation, wildfire smoke and increased pollutant loads associated with floods, droughts and other environmental catastrophes. Shifts in the exposome, including contamination of water systems and food chains, further link temperature-related barrier injury to rising rates of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs). Clinical and epidemiological evidence supports associations between heat waves and disease exacerbations, between cold exposure and infectious or allergic responses, and between altered weather patterns and growing prevalence of NCDs. This review synthesizes mechanistic, environmental and epidemiological data to highlight extreme temperatures as critical drivers of epithelial barrier dysfunction and global disease burden.

papers.title: LandSyMM-IMOGEN v1.0: a coupled land-system and climate-emulator framework for tracing land-management greenhouse-gas emissions through climate to ecosystem responses
papers.abstract: Abstract. Land use, management, and land-cover change account for approximately a quarter of anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Despite substantial progress in Earth system modelling, the CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O emissions arising specifically from land management remain incompletely accounted for, preventing closure of the feedback between management decisions, the resulting emissions, the climate response, and ecosystem impacts. Here we extend the LandSyMM modelling framework by coupling it with the intermediate-complexity climate emulator IMOGEN and by integrating IPCC Tier-1 agricultural-emission methods. The framework assembles a sector-complete, bottom-up emissions dataset by combining the SSP-RCP background emissions with socioeconomically driven land-use projections, Tier-1 agricultural emissions, and process-based land-biosphere fluxes. These emissions (not prescribed concentrations) drive the emulator, which converts them to atmospheric GHG concentrations and radiative forcing, and pattern-scales the result into climate, which in turn forces a final simulation of the resulting ecosystem trajectories. Simulating the historical period and five Shared Socioeconomic Pathway-Representative Concentration Pathway (SSP-RCP) scenarios (SSP1-2.6 through SSP5-8.5), we evaluate the framework's reproduction of historical agricultural emissions, integrated emission and concentration trajectories, as well as climate-forcing patterns against established inventories (FAOSTAT, EDGAR), observational concentration records and global budgets, and the Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project phase 3b (ISIMIP-3b) climate reference. LandSyMM reproduces historical agricultural GHG emissions across major source categories within the source-level uncertainty of the Tier-1 method (1970–2020): the agricultural CH₄ aggregate runs +19 % high owing to IPCC default emission factors for the dominant livestock sources, while the N₂O aggregate is near-balanced against FAOSTAT. With the complete natural-source terms included, the integrated emissions match the observationally constrained global budgets to within a few per cent at the present day. The prognostic atmospheric CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O concentration records are reproduced to within about 7 ppm, 50 ppb, and 6 ppb (root-mean-square over the historical period), subject to small end-of-period offsets. Relative to the unmodified reference-scenario anthropogenic emissions with the emulator's default natural baseline, our bottom-up integrated emissions – substituting the IPCC Tier-1 agricultural and LPJ-GUESS land-biosphere terms – diverge increasingly over the century: by 2100 the integrated CH₄ is 14 to 71 % higher, while the explicit terrestrial carbon sink lowers the net CO₂ source by about 1 to 5 Pg C yr⁻¹. The emulated climate reproduces the ISIMIP-3b reference closely in both spatial pattern (r ≈ 0.98 for temperature) and global-mean magnitude (within about 0.3 K across scenarios and analysis windows), leaving only a small residual regional mean-state difference that is near-neutral in the global mean. Returned to LPJ-GUESS, the two configurations settle to slightly different absolute carbon pools because they respond to different observation-based baseline climatologies (an initial-condition effect rather than a coupling signal), but compared on the meaningful basis of their changes over time they track each other closely, on a geography closely shared with the reference and with small, mixed crop-yield differences. Passed through IMOGEN, this lower net CO₂ source outweighs the higher CH₄ and lowers projected global-land-mean warming by about 0.2 to 0.5 K – a cooling that is largest (about 0.5 K) under the low-forcing SSP1-2.6 – and an identical-emulator diagnostic confirms this emission-pathway feedback is independent of the baseline climatology. The framework establishes a traceable platform for investigating the climate-ecosystem consequences of land-management GHG emissions, enabling explicit attribution of ecosystem responses to specific agricultural management practices.

papers.title: Shallow landslide diagnostics for Southern California
papers.abstract: Shallow landslides are significant natural hazards in the mountainous regions of Southern California during anomalously wet winter seasons, posing substantial risks to life and property. Better understanding and operational prediction of the atmospheric and land-surface conditions leading to the initiation of these impactful events are critical for mitigating life loss and reducing damage costs. This study aims to characterize and provide templates for operational prediction of the triggering conditions of shallow landslides in Southern California with the application of the MHEBC, a decade-long, high-resolution, prototype dataset of quantitative precipitation estimates. This dataset has region-specific calibration and is the result of methodologies tailored to capture the orographic signal of precipitation, which is a key element for the generation of the precipitation associated with landslide occurrence in this region. Using recorded landslide events from the California Geological Survey Reported Landslides Database, rainfall thresholds for landslide occurrence are derived on the basis of the MHEBC dataset. Significant quality control was necessary for both rainfall and landslide databases before high-quality data input could be provided for the analysis. Observed local landslide data availability is typically limited worldwide, and Southern California is no exception. For such conditions, estimates of landslide occurrence are obtained using manually-derived precipitation thresholds, following well defined operational procedures. In addition, a Random Forest (RF) machine-learning model and a few of its variants were applied to the same high quality but limited dataset to examine its utility for operational prediction under typically limited data. Under a variety of performance measures the automated RF does only marginally better than the well-established manual threshold procedure. Overall, the analysis demonstrates a valuable hydrological land surface application of the MHEBC dataset and provides insights towards skillful regional landslide forecasting in Southern California.

papers.title: The impact of defaunation on nature’s contributions to people in the Pan-Amazon: a scoping synthesis of evidence and research gaps
papers.abstract: The Amazon biome faces intensifying threats to its biodiversity, including accelerated deforestation, overexploitation of wildlife, fires, agricultural expansion, mining, and infrastructure construction. Understanding how the scientific literature has evaluated faunal contributions to Nature’s Contributions to People (NCP) is important for informing future conservation and research priorities. Through a broad scoping review, we aimed to (1) assess the ecological role and Nature’s Contributions to People (NCP) provided by terrestrial and freshwater faunas in the Pan-Amazon; (2) synthesize the current state of knowledge and critically examine how these potential associations have been explored and documented in the literature; and (3) identify any knowledge gaps and areas requiring further research. We analysed the data qualitatively and using descriptive statistics. Our synthesis of 135 studies reveals a research bias toward the interaction between fauna and provisioning services, such as hunting and fishing, while cultural services and the role of invertebrates remain critically underrepresented. Similarly, the role of faunal declines in ecosystem changes remains understudied in the empirical literature. Geographically, studies cluster in Brazil and Peru, leaving gaps across much of the Amazon. The reviewed studies frequently documented biodiversity declines associated with overexploitation, habitat loss, and climate change. This decline is associated with widespread depletion of faunas, which may disrupt ecosystem functioning and human well-being. Defaunation is linked to changes in ecological relationships that can alter ecosystem processes and, consequently, potentially impact human well-being. We urgently need to recognize the critical role of wildlife and build political will to develop targeted policies and funding mechanisms that address faunistic loss in terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems alongside forest cover. papers.title: A world in chaos: Who engineers, amplifies and exploits crisis on the road to 2030?
papers.abstract: This documentary essay examines how political, military, environmental, and public-health crises are deliberately produced, amplified, or exploited, and how their consequences may shape governance on the road to 2030. Drawing on institutional records, declassified archives, scientific and humanitarian assessments, contemporary reporting, and the author’s earlier writings, it analyses developments from June 2025 to 20 October 2026 through a critical historical and biblical lens. Cases involving political unrest, Ukraine, Sudan, the Israel–Iran confrontation, natural hazards, and disease emergencies reveal distinct but interacting pathways of intentional harm, institutional opportunism, and social vulnerability. Historical records of covert intervention establish that certain forms of manipulation are real; they do not substantiate a single hidden command directing every contemporary disaster. Public agendas for international coordination, digital identity, artificial intelligence, and financial interoperability likewise create opportunities for cooperation alongside risks of surveillance, exclusion, and concentrated power. The essay evaluates the unverified letter attributed to Albert Pike, the biblical accounts of Isaac and Ishmael, and Persia’s appearance in Ezekiel 38–39 without equating contested claims or eschatological interpretations with historical proof. It also considers military adaptation during the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts while distinguishing operational learning from a predetermined world-war strategy. Retrospective comparison with the author’s pre-2025 warnings identifies thematic continuities but no verified prophetic timetable. A four-part framework distinguishes direct orchestration, organized amplification, opportunistic exploitation, and structural convergence. The essay concludes that Christian preparedness requires biblical fidelity, evidence-based discernment, institutional accountability, compassion for victims, and watchfulness without date-setting.

papers.title: Post-event information in calendar-year satellite products inflates landslide susceptibility assessments
papers.abstract: Annual satellite products, such as the AlphaEarth Foundations and TESSERA embeddings, summarize a calendar year, so the product of a landslide's event year also contains post-event observations. We audited this post-event information in 18 dated events (7 earthquakes, 11 rainstorms; 61,402 landslides), changing only the input year within each event and keeping the points, spatial folds, models and bootstrap clusters fixed. Replacing the prior-year AlphaEarth product with the event-year product raised the out-of-fold AUC by 0.087 (95% CI 0.065–0.110; all 18 events) for a point model and by 0.071 (0.048–0.093) for a patch CNN. The point-model gain was 0.085 after subtracting each event's drift between two pre-event years. On complete maps, the event-year input added on average 0.21–0.22 of the landslide area to the map's top 10% (9 of 9 events; up to 0.46). A training-year × prediction-year decomposition traced the inflation to models that learn the event's surface changes, chiefly its landslide scars; event-year inputs used only at prediction did not inflate within-event scores on average. The inflation grew with the post-event fraction of the year, reaching half its full size when 23–39% of the year followed the event; this relation survived corrections for recovery. TESSERA and plain Sentinel-2 composites behaved alike. In forward tests in three regions, models trained on earlier landslides scored 0.02–0.11 higher AUC on the new event with event-year inputs, whereas legitimate pre-event embeddings helped mainly near earlier landslides. Studies should use only products whose year ends before the event.

papers.title: The Nexus Between Agriculture, Cattle Breeding and Climate Change in The Island of Crete, Greece
papers.abstract: Climate change threatens human prosperity as it affects many economic sectors including food production. Agriculture, cattle breeding and climate change are interrelated and interconnected affecting each other. Agriculture in Crete was in the past an important pillar in the local economy while nowadays its role has been decreased. The linkages between food production and climate change in the island of Crete, Greece have been analyzed. It has been indicated that climate change affects crops, trees and cattle breeding in Crete. These impacts are mainly negative while the increase in atmospheric CO2 concentration has positive impacts on plants’ photosynthesis and pastures’ productivity. Current agricultural and cattle breeding practices in the island have negative impacts on climate change increasing the emissions of greenhouse gases such as CO2, CH4, N2O and NH3. Therefore, climate change and food production in Crete are interconnected and interlinked affecting each other. Therefore, there is urgent need to develop policies and measures to reduce the impacts of agriculture and cattle breeding on climate change in the island and adapt the local food production systems to the new climate conditions. Our results could be useful to policy makers, public authorities and to all stakeholders of food production systems in the island.

papers.title: Variation of total organic carbon concentrations in rainwater in Hanoi City, Vietnam
papers.abstract: Organic carbon in precipitation represents an important pathway linking atmospheric processes with terrestrial and aquatic carbon cycling, yet data from rapidly urbanizing tropical and subtropical cities remain scarce. This study investigated total organic carbon (TOC) concentrations in 264 rainwater samples collected from 21 wards across Hanoi, Vietnam, between May 2023 and December 2025. TOC concentrations ranged from 0.41 to 17.72 mgC.L-1, with an average of 3.75±2.94 mgC.L-1, exceeding mean values previously reported for Asia and global continental regions. Significant seasonal variability was observed, with TOC concentrations consistently higher during the dry season than the rainy season, reflecting the dominant influence of rainfall dilution and atmospheric washout processes. The study also detected an upward trend in annual mean TOC concentrations over the study period, suggesting increasing contributions from anthropogenic emissions. Despite Hanoi receiving relatively high annual rainfall, elevated TOC concentrations indicate that urban activities remain an important source of atmospheric organic carbon available for wet deposition. This study provides critical baseline data to improve regional and global estimates of wet organic carbon deposition, advance understanding of carbon cycling in urban environments, and support strategies for air quality management and sustainable rainwater use.

papers.title: Impact of heatwaves on sources and transformations of ambient volatile organic compounds
papers.abstract: Abstract. Heatwaves are increasingly frequent, intense, and prolonged under climate change, affecting atmospheric chemistry and secondary air pollution. Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are key precursors of ozone (O3) and secondary organic aerosol (SOA), yet the impacts of heatwaves on VOC-related processes remain not fully integrated. This review synthesizes advances in heatwave impacts on VOC emissions, source contributions, transformation, and secondary pollution. Based on 287 publications (~67% from 2020–2026), observations show that heatwaves increase total ambient VOCs, but dominant compounds vary by city and reflect local emissions. Temperature-sensitive anthropogenic sources (solvent use, volatile chemical products, fuel storage, vehicle evaporation) increase strongly, whereas combustion sources are less temperature-dependent. Biogenic VOC emissions, especially isoprene and monoterpenes, respond nonlinearly to temperature and are modulated by plant physiology, water stress, and species-specific storage/synthesis. Heatwaves also enhance atmospheric oxidation through increased photolysis and radical production, altering VOC oxidation, radical cycling, O3 formation regimes, and gas-particle partitioning. Enhanced emissions and oxidation can promote O3 and SOA formation, but net responses depend on VOC-NOx sensitivity, peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) chemistry, product volatility, partitioning, reactive uptake, and particle-phase diffusion. Observations, experiments, emission parameterizations, source apportionment, inverse modeling, and chemical transport models provide complementary evidence, but uncertainties remain in temperature-dependent emissions, semi-volatile/intermediate-volatility organic compounds (S/IVOCs) oxidation, multiphase chemistry, and observational constraints. Future research should integrate high-resolution measurements, source apportionment, inverse modeling, and process-based models across heatwave events to quantify source-specific temperature responses and improve predictions of VOC-driven secondary pollution.

papers.title: HTAP3-OPNS: ozone, PM, nitrogen and sulphur deposition – multi-model experiments to support the revision of the CLRTAP Gothenburg Protocol
papers.abstract: Abstract. HTAP3-OPNS is a multi-model exercise designed to support the revision of the Gothenburg Protocol under the UNECE Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (CLRTAP). Using an ensemble of Chemical Transport Models (CTMs) and Chemistry-Climate Models (CCMs), this study investigates the long-range transport and impacts of ground-level ozone, particulate matter (PM), and nitrogen and sulphur deposition across different global regions. The project aims to assess the contributions of regional versus extra-regional emission sources, evaluate the suitability of current models, and project changes in air pollution under future emission scenarios and climate conditions. A series of perturbation simulations will enable the development of an ensemble emulator to explore and evaluate potential mitigation strategies efficiently. This paper outlines the scientific and policy questions motivating the study, describes the experimental design, including input datasets, model configurations, and required outputs, and discusses methodologies for data handling and analysis. The results will provide crucial insights for policy decisions aiming to improve air quality, protect human health, and protect ecosystems worldwide.

papers.title: Understanding and reducing methane emissions: insights into anthropogenic, natural sources, and novel mitigation techniques
papers.abstract: Abstract Methane (CH 4 ) is a potent, short-lived greenhouse gas. Among the major well-mixed greenhouse gases, it ranks second only to carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) in its contribution to anthropogenic radiative forcing. Although methane remains in the atmosphere for approximately 12 years, its 100-year global warming potential (GWP100) is approximately 27–30 times greater than that of CO 2 (IPCC AR6), making rapid mitigation a critical near-term climate strategy. This review synthesizes current understanding of methane emissions from anthropogenic and natural sources, evaluates sector-specific mitigation potentials, and critically examines emerging reduction technologies. Fossil fuel extraction, agriculture (particularly enteric fermentation), and waste management collectively account for the majority of anthropogenic methane emissions, with significant variability in mitigation feasibility and cost-effectiveness. Advanced methane monitoring systems, feed additives, biochar applications, leak detection technologies, and microbial interventions show considerable mitigation potential but face technical limitations, high implementation costs, infrastructure barriers, and scalability challenges. We emphasize sectoral prioritization, policy integration, and trade-offs associated with mitigation strategies. Immediate methane reductions offer substantial co-benefits, including improved air quality and public health, while directly supporting Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 13, 7, and 12). Strategic, evidence-based methane mitigation represents one of the most effective pathways to limit near-term warming and accelerate climate stabilization.

papers.title: Ecological restoration of the land-sea interface: practices, challenges, and prospects in the Yellow River Delta
papers.abstract: The ecological degradation of the Yellow River Delta is driven by the coupled effects of multiple land–river–sea stressors, including altered fluvial water and sediment regimes, seawater intrusion, biological invasions, and intensive human activities. However, existing restoration practices remain largely component-specific and therefore have limited capacity to address these interacting pressures. This review synthesizes multidisciplinary evidence to elucidate the major degradation processes, trace the evolution of restoration research, and characterize emerging synergistic restoration practices in the Yellow River Delta. The analysis reveals an increasing research emphasis on ecological connectivity, multi-objective coordination, and system-oriented restoration alongside earlier attention to water–sediment regulation and single-factor restoration. Based on representative practices, we further identify three complementary dimensions of synergistic restoration: elemental synergy, integrating hydrology, salinity, topography, and biological processes; spatial synergy, linking watershed, landscape, estuarine, and nearshore scales; and objective synergy, integrating invasive-species control with native habitat reconstruction. Building on these findings, we propose a resilience-oriented restoration framework that integrates Nature-based Solutions, Digital Twin technologies, and cross-scale adaptive management. This framework provides a systematic basis for coordinating ecological processes, restoration actions, and management institutions in the Yellow River Delta and offers transferable insights for other rapidly changing deltaic ecosystems.

papers.title: The effect of temperature on fertility: a province-level analysis of monthly total fertility rates in Italy in 2003–2022
papers.abstract: Abstract Long-term climate change has increased the frequency and intensity of high-temperature weather events, which in turn affect human health and wellbeing. Warmer temperatures are reported to affect both reproductive health and behaviors, possibly reducing birth rates. In a low-fertility context, the potential negative impact that climate change might have on fertility is consequential. This study focuses on Italy, a low-fertility country disproportionately affected by climate change, with sharp regional disparities in both climate zones and economic development. Matching monthly birth registration data for the period 2003 to 2022 with E-OBS, ERA-5 and CAMS meteorological data, we analyze the relationship between heat exposure and total fertility rates in 107 Italian provinces (corresponding to the NUTS-3 classification). Results show that exposure to hot days, which are defined as days with a mean temperature above 25 °C, has a relatively immediate impact on conception probabilities as it reduces the total fertility rate nine months later. Additional analyses revealed that the largest effect of heat on fertility occurs in above-average GDP provinces and provinces with lower-than-average healthcare workforce availability.
